June 9, 2026 
 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0062-P 
P.O. Box 8013 
Baltimore, MD 21244-8013 
 
Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified 
Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
I am writing on behalf of the HIV Medicine Association (HIVMA) to provide comments 
regarding the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule on 
interoperability standards and prior authorization. HIVMA represents nearly 6,000 physicians, 
researchers, scientists and other healthcare professionals who work on the frontlines of the HIV 
epidemic providing prevention and care and conducting research in communities across the 
country. 
 
Prior authorization is a growing challenge for people who need HIV prevention and treatment 
medications. A recent paper published by HIVMA outlined the clinical and administrative 
barriers that inappropriate and burdensome prior authorization processes place on access to HIV 
medications.1 Opaque and lengthy prior authorization decision timelines can lead to delayed 
medication access and disruptions in treatment that can result in increased likelihood of drug 
resistance and disease progression. HIV providers have described the administrative burden of 
prior authorization as consuming valuable time and resources, with individual prior authorization 
requests taking up hours or even full days of staff time depending on the complexity of the 
request. Prior authorization requests for long-acting injectable therapies can be the most onerous 
and time-consuming, which is concerning given the dynamic HIV pipeline with new long-acting 
products on the way.  
 
We broadly support the proposed interoperability standards and extension of prior authorization 
timelines to prescription drugs. These provisions will help to alleviate the administrative burdens 
 
1 HIVMA, Prior Authorization and HIV Medications: Considerations for State Policymakers (January 2026), 
https://www.hivma.org/~/link/1e2fc39f5d5a45cf849a9e309e3ad30a.aspx 
2 
associated with prior authorization and ensure timely access to HIV services. We urge CMS to 
consider the following comments to build on the proposed protections and ensure that the final 
rule and any future rulemaking on prior authorization supports access to clinically necessary HIV 
prevention and treatment.   
 
Impacted Payers 
 
We urge CMS to expand the ruleâ€™s requirements to additional payers.  
 
The 2024 final rule applied interoperability standards and prior authorization decision timelines 
to Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service (FFS) programs, Medicaid and CHIP managed care plans, 
and issuers of Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) on the federally-facilitated exchanges (FFEs).2 We 
support CMSâ€™s proposal to extend application of these protections to QHP issuers offering plans 
on the Federally-facilitated Small Business Health Options Program (FF-SHOP) as we think this 
will create consistency across QHP offerings. We believe that CMS should extend these 
protections to QHP issuers offering plans on the state-based marketplaces (SBMs) as well. While 
we recognize that it may require different statutory authority, we urge CMS to work 
collaboratively with the Department of Labor to assess whether similar prior authorization and 
interoperability requirements could be applied to self-funded ERISA plans. 
 
Interoperability and API Standards 
 
We support the proposed interoperability and API standards, but urge CMS to ensure 
transparency when prescription drugs covered as a medical benefit. 
 
We understand that prescription drugs covered as a medical benefit warrant a different electronic 
transmission standard than prescription drugs covered as pharmacy benefit. However, we urge 
CMS to ensure that the quality, timeliness, and specificity of prior authorization criteria and 
other information is comparable regardless of what benefit category a plan uses to cover the 
drug. Long-acting injectable medications for HIV treatment and prevention are often covered as 
a medical benefit, and providers have reported challenges accessing medical benefit coverage 
information, including prior authorization criteria.3 
 
Prior Authorization Timelines 
 
We urge CMS to apply the most protective decision timelines across all payers.  
 
Efficient adjudication of prior authorization requests is critical for timely access to life-saving 
HIV medications. Studies show that early access to antiretroviral therapy helps to support viral 
 
2 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), 
https://www.cms.gov/priorities/burden-reduction/overview/interoperability/policies-regulations/cms-
interoperability-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f 
3 Hack J, Tarfa A, Sayles H, Fadul N. High Acceptability but Persistent Barriers to Implementation of Long-acting 
Injectable Antiretrovirals: A Nationwide Cross-sectional Survey of Ryan White Clinics in the United States. Open 
Forum Infect Dis. 2025 Mar 28;12(4):ofaf192. doi: 10.1093/ofid/ofaf192. PMID: 40242071; PMCID: 
PMC12002010. 
3 
suppression for people living with HIV, which is an important HIV outcome measure.4 When 
someone is virally suppressed, not only is their individual health protected, but that person also 
cannot transmit the virus sexually to other people.5 We support the proposed ruleâ€™s application of 
the prior authorization decision timelines adopted in the 2024 rule for non-drug items and 
services for Medicaid and Medicare Advantage to QHP issuers in FFEs.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
To ensure consistency across payers, we also urge CMS to adopt the most protective 
standard for prescription drugs (the 24-hour standard for any request in Medicaid FFS 
and Medicaid and CHIP managed care) to QHP issuers. Many issuers sell products across 
Medicaid, Medicare Managed care, and QHP markets and will be easily able to apply a 
consistent and uniform standard for prior authorization decisions across markets. Policy 
consistency would also ensure that protections donâ€™t shift as individuals move in and out of 
different forms of coverage. 
 
We also support the requirement that impacted payers provide a specific denial reason for 
a prior authorization prescription drug denial starting October 1, 2027. This aligns with an 
identical requirement CMS had included in the 2024 interoperability rule that applies to non-
drug items and services. While requiring denial reasons is an important protection, CMS should 
also require impacted payers to include the specific clinical criteria used to make the prior 
authorization determination, along with the denial reason. This additional information will 
enable providers and patients to submit more detailed appeals, especially in cases where a denial 
conflicts with clinical standards of care for HIV. 
 
Prior Authorization Reporting 
 
We support the prior authorization reporting metrics CMS has proposed and believe there 
are additional metrics that could increase transparency and accountability. 
 
4 Hoenigl, M., Chaillon, A., Moore, D. et al. Rapid HIV Viral Load Suppression in those Initiating Antiretroviral 
Therapy at First Visit after HIV Diagnosis. Sci Rep 6, 32947 (2016) https://doi.org/10.1038/srep32947. 
5 HIV.gov, Viral Suppression and an Undetectable Viral Load (accessed May 2026), https://www.hiv.gov/hiv-
basics/staying-in-hiv-care/hiv-treatment/viral-suppression  
4 
 
The additional proposed reporting metrics plans must include on their public websites are a step 
toward greater transparency into what has historically been an opaque practice and will help to 
shed light on plan prior authorization trends. However as proposed, the rule does not require data 
to be disaggregated by service type. Without this detail, the public (and regulators) cannot see 
what proportion of prescription drugs and devices are subject to prior authorization and what 
relative denial/approval rates are compared to other service categories. For HIV, it would be 
helpful to know which drug categories/classes or even which specific antiretroviral 
medications are more likely to be subject to prior authorization and/or are more likely to 
be denied. This type of information could help point to possible discriminatory plan 
designs.  
 
The proposed rule also does not include any metrics to capture usage of artificial intelligence 
(AI) tools, despite the increasing prevalence of AI use to aid in prior authorization adjudication 
and CMS should consider adding metrics to capture this. Data collected on AI could include how 
carriers are using AI and machine learning tools for prior authorization requests (e.g., to evaluate 
submitted medical record data or to make a recommendation for approval or denial), which AI 
models they are using, and what safeguards and data governance systems issuers and third-party 
data vendors are using to guard against inaccurate models, bias, and discrimination based on 
protected classes. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) has developed 
an extensive survey tool and AI evaluation tool that could provide specific data queries.6  
 
Finally, while we support the requirement for metrics to be reported on plan websites, CMS 
should also use this granular prior authorization data as part of federal monitoring and oversight 
activities. The data that plans will have to report on prior authorization could illuminate 
consumer protection compliance gaps, particularly with regard to inappropriate use of prior 
authorization in contradiction to evidence-based standards of care and medical necessity 
requirements. CMS should use this data to ensure compliance with federal law. This data could 
also help CMS to pursue additional prior authorization reforms that aim to address more 
substantive challenges in addition to the process challenges more squarely addressed in the 
proposed rule. 
 
Step Therapy RFI 
 
We urge CMS to address step therapy in future rulemaking. 
 
Step therapy is never an appropriate utilization management technique for HIV. Requiring 
people with HIV or at increased risk of HIV to â€œfailâ€ on a particular regimen before 
accessing a regimen their provider recommends can have dire individual and public health 
consequences.7 We appreciate the call for comments from interested parties on whether and how 
APIs can be used to ensure access to relevant step therapy requirements, including criteria and 
service use history from previous payers to current payers. We believe that adding step therapy 
 
6 NAIC Big Data and AI (H) Working Group, AI System Evaluation Tool 4.0 and Health AI/ML Survey Report, 
available at https://content.naic.org/committees/h/big-data-artificial-intelligence-wg 
7 Baumgardner J, Huber C, Kabiri M, Yoon L, Chou J, Romley J. Modeling the impacts of restrictive formularies on 
patients with HIV. Am J Manag Care. 2018 Jul;24(8 Spec No.):SP322-SP328. PMID: 30020747. 
5 
information to API requirements will be useful for providers and people living and at increased 
risk for HIV. This will allow patients and providers to see any specific step requirements for 
each HIV regimen. For state and federal regulators, this information may help to better 
understand how step therapy is being used in order to craft consumer protections that prohibit its 
use when it interferes with clinically recommended care and treatment. CMS should also 
consider adding more specific definitions for prior authorization and step therapy. In practice, 
while some plans may classify step therapy as a specific type of utilization management, others 
fold step therapy criteria into broader prior authorization policies without labeling them step 
therapy. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Please reach out to the HIVMA Executive Director 
Andrea Weddle at aweddle@hivma.org with questions regarding our comments.  
 
Sincerely 
 
 
 
 
Anna K. Person, MD, FIDSA 
Chair, HIV Medicine Association

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** HIV Medicine Association (HIVMA); signed by Anna K. Person, MD, FIDSA, Chair
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** HIVMA represents nearly 6,000 physicians, researchers, scientists, and other healthcare professionals involved in HIV prevention, care, and research.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

HIVMA broadly supports extending interoperability standards and prior authorization timelines to prescription drugs, emphasizing that burdensome PA can delay HIV prevention and treatment medications and create serious individual and public health risks. It asks CMS to expand payer scope, require comparable transparency for medical-benefit drugs, apply the most protective 24-hour decision standard across payers, strengthen denial and reporting requirements, and address step therapy in future rulemaking.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; API-USAGE-METRICS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations; references CMS-0057-F, the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule.
- **Standards referenced:** API standards; electronic transmission standards; prior authorization APIs; no specific FHIR IG or NCPDP standard named.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Scope of Impacted Payers**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS / GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Consistent protections should apply across QHP offerings and should not shift when individuals move between coverage types.
- **Specific request:** Finalize FF-SHOP applicability, extend protections to state-based marketplace QHPs, and collaborate with the Department of Labor on possible application to self-funded ERISA plans.

**Topic 2: Comparable Transparency for Medical-Benefit HIV Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Long-acting injectable HIV medications are often covered under the medical benefit, and providers report difficulty accessing coverage and PA criteria.
- **Specific request:** Ensure quality, timeliness, and specificity of PA criteria and information are comparable regardless of medical or pharmacy benefit coverage.

**Topic 3: Prior Authorization Timelines and Denial Reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS / PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Delays in HIV medication access can disrupt treatment, contribute to drug resistance or disease progression, and affect viral suppression.
- **Specific request:** Apply the Medicaid 24-hour standard for prescription drug PA to QHP issuers and require denial reasons to include the specific clinical criteria used.

**Topic 4: Reporting Metrics and Oversight**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Current proposed metrics improve transparency but may not reveal prescription drug/device patterns, HIV drug class impacts, or AI-related bias and governance risks.
- **Specific request:** Disaggregate PA metrics by service type and, where useful, drug category/class or specific antiretroviral; add AI-use metrics; use reported data for federal monitoring and enforcement.

**Topic 5: Step Therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** HIVMA states step therapy is inappropriate for HIV because forcing patients to fail a regimen can have serious health and public health consequences.
- **Specific request:** Address step therapy in future rulemaking, add API-accessible step therapy requirements and prior service-use history, and define prior authorization and step therapy more precisely.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** HIVMA identifies challenges for medical-benefit drug PA, especially access to coverage information and criteria for long-acting injectable HIV medications.
- **S15:** HIVMA directly addresses medical versus pharmacy benefit distinctions and asks for comparable quality, timeliness, and specificity of PA information regardless of benefit category.
- **S16:** HIVMA supports specific denial reasons for prescription drug PA denials beginning October 1, 2027.
- **S17:** HIVMA asks CMS to require the specific clinical criteria used in a denial, which would make denial information more actionable for appeals.
- **S20:** HIVMA urges CMS to apply the 24-hour Medicaid prescription drug decision standard to QHP issuers.
- **S21:** HIVMA supports extending PA decision timelines to prescription drugs and to QHP issuers on FFEs.
- **S29-S35:** HIVMA supports proposed reporting metrics but asks for more granular reporting by service type, drug class, specific antiretroviral, AI usage, and federal oversight use.
- **S40:** HIVMA supports extending interoperability and PA protections to FF-SHOP QHP issuers and asks CMS to consider state-based marketplaces as well.
- **S49:** HIVMA indirectly addresses cross-market consistency and payer scope, including issuers operating across Medicaid, Medicare managed care, and QHP markets.
- **S66-S82:** HIVMA responds to the step therapy RFI by arguing step therapy should not be used for HIV and that APIs should expose step therapy requirements and prior service-use history.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Extend the rule's protections to FF-SHOP QHP issuers as proposed.
2. Expand similar protections to state-based marketplace QHPs where possible.
3. Work with the Department of Labor on similar requirements for self-funded ERISA plans.
4. Ensure medical-benefit prescription drugs have comparable PA transparency to pharmacy-benefit drugs.
5. Apply the 24-hour Medicaid prescription drug PA decision standard to QHP issuers.
6. Require denial notices to include the clinical criteria used in the PA determination.
7. Disaggregate PA metrics by service type and, for HIV, by drug category/class or specific antiretroviral medication where appropriate.
8. Add reporting metrics on AI and machine learning use in PA adjudication, including safeguards and data governance.
9. Use reported PA data for federal monitoring, compliance, and future reforms.
10. Address step therapy in future rulemaking and expose step therapy requirements through APIs.
11. Define prior authorization and step therapy more specifically.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Delayed access to HIV medications, administrative burden, opaque PA timelines, medical-benefit coverage information gaps, inconsistent payer protections, insufficient metrics, AI bias, and step therapy use in HIV.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Drug resistance, disease progression, reduced viral suppression, HIV transmission risk, discriminatory plan designs, and delays in clinically recommended care.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Coverage category differences, inconsistent payer markets, opaque criteria, AI governance gaps, and plans folding step therapy criteria into broader PA policies without clear labeling.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** HIVMA represents nearly 6,000 professionals; PA requests may take hours or full days of staff time; early antiretroviral therapy supports viral suppression; viral suppression prevents sexual transmission.
- **Studies or research referenced:** HIVMA January 2026 paper on PA and HIV medications; Hack et al. 2025 on long-acting injectable antiretroviral implementation barriers; Hoenigl et al. 2016 on rapid viral load suppression; HIV.gov on viral suppression; NAIC AI evaluation resources; Baumgardner et al. 2018 on restrictive formularies for HIV.
- **Examples provided:** Long-acting injectable HIV therapies, antiretroviral medications subject to PA or denial, AI use in PA adjudication, and step therapy requirements embedded within PA policies.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** People living with or at increased risk for HIV, HIV clinicians, QHP issuers, Medicaid and CHIP programs, MA plans, pharmacies, medical-benefit administrators, regulators, and vendors using AI tools.
- **Economic implications:** Not quantified; HIVMA emphasizes staff time burden, potential avoidable disease progression, and oversight value from granular data.
- **Technical feasibility:** HIVMA supports API standards but requests added data granularity, cross-benefit transparency, and AI reporting to make the systems clinically useful and accountable.
- **Patient care impact:** High; faster and more transparent PA for HIV medications supports viral suppression, avoids treatment interruption, and protects public health.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, evidence-based, and policy-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We broadly support the proposed interoperability standards and extension of prior authorization timelines to prescription drugs." - Context: Overall support for the proposed rule.
2. "Opaque and lengthy prior authorization decision timelines can lead to delayed medication access" - Context: Rationale for stronger timelines and transparency.
3. "apply the most protective decision timelines across all payers" - Context: Request for a 24-hour standard beyond Medicaid.
4. "Step therapy is never an appropriate utilization management technique for HIV." - Context: Future rulemaking recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - HIVMA emphasizes shorter timelines and a 24-hour standard for prescription drug PA.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment describes PA requests consuming hours or full days of staff time.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Administrative burden on HIV providers is a central concern.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The comment addresses access to HIV prevention and treatment and potential discriminatory plan designs.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - HIVMA supports APIs but requests more detailed, clinically useful PA, step therapy, and AI information.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Timely access to HIV medications is the primary patient-care concern.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - HIVMA notes that extending requirements to state-based marketplaces and ERISA plans may require different authority or DOL collaboration.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment asks CMS to work with DOL and use reported data for oversight.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - HIVMA specifically addresses long-acting injectables often covered under the medical benefit.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - The comment asks for denial criteria, granular metrics, AI reporting, and step therapy visibility.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - It discusses current PA, appeals, AI adjudication, and step therapy practices.
